sections.name: General Knowledge / Current Affairs of India and Goa

p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Vaccines are among the most successful tools public health has ever possessed, yet their success contains a peculiar weakness. When a disease such as measles becomes rare, parents no longer see its effects with their own eyes, and the small, visible risks of an injection begin to loom larger than the invisible danger it prevents. Hesitancy, in this sense, is partly a product of achievement. It is rarely the result of simple ignorance. Many hesitant parents have read a great deal; what they lack is not information but confidence in those who provide it.

For this reason, campaigns that merely repeat statistics often fail, and campaigns that ridicule doubters do worse, hardening suspicion into identity. Studies of successful immunisation drives point instead to the quiet authority of familiar figures: the local health worker who has visited a household for years, the doctor who takes time to answer a question rather than dismiss it, the community leader who is seen to vaccinate his own children. Trust of this kind is slow to build and quick to destroy, and a single poorly handled adverse event, concealed rather than explained, can undo the work of a decade. Honesty about rare side effects, far from undermining confidence, is often what sustains it.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Corruption is usually imagined as a dramatic act: an envelope of cash passed beneath a table, a contract awarded in exchange for a bribe. Far more common, and in some ways more corrosive, is the quiet conflict of interest. An official who decides on a road alignment that happens to raise the value of his brother's land, or a doctor who prescribes a costly test at a laboratory in which she holds shares, may never accept a rupee from anyone. They may even believe sincerely that their decision was correct on its merits. The difficulty is that no one, including the decision-maker, can be sure. Self-interest rarely announces itself; it works by tilting judgement a few degrees in a convenient direction.

For this reason, the ethics of public life cannot rest on good intentions alone. A sound system does not ask whether a particular official is honest; it arranges matters so that honesty does not have to be taken on trust. Interests are declared in advance, those with a stake step aside from decisions that touch it, and records are kept open to scrutiny. Such rules can seem fussy or even insulting to people of integrity. But they protect the honest as much as they restrain the dishonest, for an official who has stepped aside cannot later be suspected of bias.

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
opts: Repeating statistics is the most effective way to raise immunisation rates.
Vaccine hesitancy is largely a problem of trust, best addressed by honest and familiar messengers.
Vaccine hesitancy is caused mainly by parents' lack of education.
Side effects of vaccines should be kept from the public to protect confidence.
questions.why: Main idea: what parents lack 'is not information but confidence in those who provide it'; successful drives rely on 'familiar figures' and honesty.

questions.q: According to the passage, campaigns that ridicule doubters:
opts: are recommended by studies of successful drives.
harden suspicion into a sense of identity.
succeed better than those that repeat statistics.
persuade most parents within a decade.
questions.why: Detail: 'campaigns that ridicule doubters do worse, hardening suspicion into identity'.

questions.q: By calling hesitancy 'partly a product of achievement', the author suggests that:
opts: better-educated parents are always more hesitant.
public health has achieved little against measles.
vaccines have become less effective over time.
the rarity of diseases brought about by vaccination makes their danger seem remote.
questions.why: Inference: 'When a disease such as measles becomes rare, parents no longer see its effects', so the vaccine's own success hides the danger.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards hesitant parents is best described as:
opts: approving, endorsing their refusal of vaccines.
understanding, treating their doubts as a matter of trust rather than foolishness.
questions.why: Tone: hesitancy 'is rarely the result of simple ignorance. Many hesitant parents have read a great deal.'

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'loom larger' means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: the visible risks of an injection seem more important 'than the invisible danger it prevents'.

questions.q: The passage is primarily about:
opts: how conflicts of interest distort judgement even without bribery, and why safeguards must not rely on trust.
the low salaries that drive officials to corruption.
the need to punish doctors who order medical tests.
the methods used to detect cash bribes in government.
questions.why: Main idea: the 'quiet conflict of interest' is 'more corrosive', so 'the ethics of public life cannot rest on good intentions alone'.

questions.q: Which example does the author use to illustrate a conflict of interest?
opts: A judge accepting gifts from a litigant.
An official refusing to declare his salary.
A doctor prescribing a costly test at a laboratory in which she holds shares.
A contractor bribing an official with cash.
questions.why: Detail: 'a doctor who prescribes a costly test at a laboratory in which she holds shares'.

questions.q: The statement that 'no one, including the decision-maker, can be sure' implies that:
opts: public decisions are usually made at random.
officials who face conflicts always lie about their motives.
self-interest can influence a decision without the person being aware of it.
evidence of conflicts is routinely destroyed.
questions.why: Inference: self-interest 'rarely announces itself; it works by tilting judgement a few degrees', so even a sincere person cannot rule it out.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards rules on declaring interests and stepping aside is:
opts: opposed, because they insult people of integrity.
dismissive, regarding them as fussy and unnecessary.
naively confident that they will end all corruption.
firmly supportive, while admitting they may seem tiresome to honest people.
questions.why: Tone: the rules 'can seem fussy or even insulting', 'But they protect the honest as much as they restrain the dishonest'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'corrosive' most nearly means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: the quiet conflict of interest slowly erodes fairness, unlike the 'dramatic act' of bribery.

questions.q: Choose the correct modal: “He ____ to play cricket every evening, but now he doesn’t.”
questions.why: 'Used to' expresses a past habit that no longer exists. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the correct transformation: “He is so weak that he cannot walk.”
opts: He is so weak to walk.
He is weak enough to walk.
He is too weak to walk.
He is very weak to walk.
questions.why: 'So ... that ... not' becomes 'too ... to'. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Find the correctly spelt word:
questions.why: Double c, double r, and ends in -ence. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Identify the part of speech of “Neither” in: “Neither of the answers is correct.”
questions.why: It stands for a noun and is followed by 'of'. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Identify the error: “He is a such brilliant student that everyone admires him.”
questions.why: The order is 'such a' + adjective + noun: 'such a brilliant student'. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Goa shares its land borders with:
questions.why: Maharashtra is to the north; Karnataka is to the east and south.

questions.q: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode) in:
questions.why: He opened the sea route from Europe to India around the Cape of Good Hope.

questions.q: Who became the first Indian, and the fastest batter in history, to hit 100 sixes in Test cricket?
questions.why: He reached the mark in the Galle Test against Sri Lanka. Aug 2026.

questions.q: Which is generally regarded as the largest freshwater lake in India?
questions.why: Wular is in Jammu and Kashmir; Chilika is a brackish-water lagoon.

questions.q: PRAGATI-50, launched by the Housing and Urban Affairs Ministry in September 2026, aims to develop 50 model cities in:
questions.why: Bhubaneswar and Puri are among the cities chosen. Sep 2026.

questions.q: At the PATWA International Travel Awards held alongside ITB Berlin in March 2026, Goa was named 'Destination of the Year –':
questions.why: Minister Rohan Khaunte also got 'Tourism Minister of the Year – Innovation (Asia)'. Mar 2026.

questions.q: Three new centipede species of the genus Rhysida, reported in October 2026, were found in the:
questions.why: Discovered by ZSI and Malabar Christian College in Kerala and Karnataka. Oct 2026.

questions.q: On which date is International Universal Health Coverage Day observed?
questions.why: Proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2017 (resolution 72/138). Dec.

questions.q: The AI-based UPI customer support launched in 2026 is built on 'FiMI', a small language model of the:
questions.why: FiMI (Finance Model for India) powers MyUPI support. Sep 2026.

questions.q: The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution by the:
questions.why: It shields land-reform laws from challenge in courts.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 9:25?
questions.why: Angle = |30×9 − 5.5×25| = 132.5°. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What comes next in the series? 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, …
questions.why: Each term is multiplied by 2. Next: 64. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Statements: Some cats are dogs. All dogs are pets. Conclusions: I. All cats are pets. II. Some pets are cats.
questions.why: Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I need not be true, II must be true. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Pointing to a man, Deepak said, "His only brother is the father of my daughter." How is the man related to Deepak?
questions.why: Draw the family tree from the statements; the answer is Brother-in-law. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In a group of 90 people, 42 like tea, 39 like coffee and 20 like neither. How many like only tea?
questions.why: Both = 42 + 39 − (90 − 20) = 11; only tea = 42 − 11 = 31. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Rahul walks 5 m West, then turns right and walks 5 m, then turns right and walks 9 m. Which direction is Rahul facing now?
questions.why: Follow each turn from the first direction: the last leg is towards the East. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Statements: All roses are flowers. No flowers are plants. Conclusions: I. All roses are plants. II. No roses are plants.
questions.why: Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I need not be true, II must be true. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What comes next in the series? 7, 26, 63, 124, 215, …
questions.why: n³ − 1 for n = 2, 3, …. Next: 342. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In how many different ways can the letters of the word REMEDY be arranged?
questions.why: 6 letters with repeats: 6! ÷ 2! = 360. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: If NURSING is written as OWUWNTN in a certain code, how is DOCTOR written in that code?
questions.why: In the code the 1st letter moves 1 place, the 2nd 2 places, the 3rd 3 places, and so on: DOCTOR → EQFXTX. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In case taking (§84), while the patient narrates his sufferings the physician should:
opts: guide the narration with questions from the start
note only the symptoms that fit the diagnosis
ask the relatives first and then the patient
keep silent and not interrupt, noting everything in the patient's own words
questions.why: §84: the physician lets the patient and friends say all they have to say without interruption and writes it down in their very expressions.

questions.q: Kent, following Swedenborg, described the vital force as:
questions.why: Kent's Lectures on Homoeopathic Philosophy call the vital force 'simple substance', an immaterial substance with formative intelligence.

questions.q: According to §201, in chronic disease the vital force develops a local malady on an external part in order to:
opts: draw attention to the internal organ affected
quiet or silence the internal disease
questions.why: §201: the vital force produces and keeps up a local symptom on a part not vital to life, to silence the internal disease; removing it externally is harmful.

questions.q: Fear that she will lose her reason, or that people will notice her confusion, is characteristic of:
questions.why: Calcarea carb: apprehension, fears losing her reason or that people will observe her confusion (Boericke).

questions.q: Antimonium tartaricum is chemically:
questions.why: Antimonium tartaricum is tartar emetic, the double tartrate of antimony and potassium; Antimonium crudum is the black sulphide.

questions.q: A suicidal impulse on seeing a knife or blood is characteristic of:
questions.why: Alumina (Boericke): suicidal tendency when seeing a knife or blood.

questions.q: A 3C potency corresponds in degree of dilution to:
questions.why: Each centesimal step equals two decimal steps (1:100 = 1:10 × 1:10), so 3C = 6X.

questions.q: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, the label of a homoeopathic medicine must bear the words:
questions.why: Rule 106-A requires the words 'Homoeopathic Medicine' on the label, along with the name, potency and other details.

questions.q: In the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, 'homoeopathic medicines' are defined in Rule:
questions.why: Rule 2(dd) defines homoeopathic medicines; Rule 30AA deals with import and Rule 67A with sale.

questions.q: Phatak's Concise Repertory of Homoeopathic Medicines was built mainly on:
questions.why: S. R. Phatak based his alphabetical repertory chiefly on C. M. Boger's Synoptic Key, enlarging it from other sources.

questions.q: The rubric 'Mind, Censorious' means:
questions.why: A censorious patient criticises and finds fault with others.

questions.q: Low serum T4 with a high TSH indicates:
questions.why: A failing thyroid removes negative feedback, so the pituitary raises TSH; in pituitary failure both T4 and TSH are low.

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin are synthesised in the:
opts: supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus
questions.why: They are made in hypothalamic neurons, carried down their axons and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary.

questions.q: The stage of the malaria parasite injected into man by the female Anopheles mosquito is the:
questions.why: Sporozoites from the mosquito's salivary glands enter the blood and go to the liver to begin exo-erythrocytic schizogony.

questions.q: A raised reticulocyte count is most typical of:
questions.why: Reticulocytosis reflects increased marrow output in response to red cell destruction or blood loss; it is low in marrow failure and deficiency states.

questions.q: The mother tincture often used in homoeopathic practice for high blood pressure is:
questions.why: Rauwolfia Q is used for hypertension; Syzygium is used for diabetes, Blatta for asthma and Berberis for renal colic.

questions.q: Diabetes following grief, with apathy, indifference, weakness and profuse, milky urine at night, calls for:
questions.why: Phosphoric acid suits debility from grief with mental apathy and profuse, frequent, milky urine.

questions.q: Which antihypertensive is contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios?
questions.why: ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic; labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the accepted antihypertensives in pregnancy.

questions.q: The birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine under the UIP should be given:
opts: any time in the first year
questions.why: Hep B birth dose is effective in preventing perinatal transmission only if given within 24 hours.

questions.q: For an infant under one month of age, the dose of BCG vaccine is:
questions.why: BCG is given intradermally in the left upper arm: 0.05 mL up to one month of age and 0.1 mL after that.

questions.q: The commonest bone fractured during birth is the:
questions.why: Clavicle fracture is the most frequent birth fracture, often in shoulder dystocia.

questions.q: In posterior dislocation of the hip, the limb is held in:
questions.why: Posterior dislocation (dashboard injury) gives flexion, adduction and internal rotation, and may injure the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: In 2020 the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP) was renamed the:
opts: National Programme for Control of Tuberculosis
questions.why: RNTCP became NTEP in 2020, reflecting the goal of eliminating TB.

questions.q: Adipocere formation results from:
opts: drying of tissues in hot, dry air
hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fat in warm, moist conditions
freezing of body water in cold climates
questions.why: Adipocere (saponification) is the conversion of fat into a soapy waxy substance in warm, moist surroundings; drying in hot air causes mummification.

questions.q: In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005), the Supreme Court held that to prosecute a doctor for criminal negligence:
opts: any error of judgement is enough
the negligence must be gross or reckless, and a private complaint should be supported by a credible medical opinion
the patient's consent form must be produced first
only a civil suit for compensation is permitted
questions.why: The judgment set guidelines protecting doctors from frivolous criminal prosecution: simple lack of care is civil; criminal liability needs gross negligence.
